analysis.one_liner: Forces wildlife agencies to leave land out of endangered species habitat areas when economics favor exclusion.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a Democrat and a Republican from Arkansas in July 2014, was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Endangered Species Act to require the Interior Department and NOAA to leave areas out of "critical habitat" designations whenever the benefits of excluding that land outweigh the benefits of including it — unless excluding it would doom the species to extinction. Today that exclusion is optional; the bill would make it mandatory. It would also require agencies to publish, with any proposed habitat designation, a detailed economic analysis covering land use, property values, water and power service, jobs, and state and local government revenues, and it would apply retroactively, reopening habitat designations finalized since October 30, 2013.
analysis.who_benefits: Private landowners and businesses whose property or projects would otherwise be restricted because it falls inside a critical habitat area. Mandatory exclusions would lift land-use restrictions wherever the economic case for exclusion is stronger than the conservation case, and the retroactive reopening provision would give landowners a new chance to challenge habitat designations that were finalized after October 2013. The bill would also hand regulated parties a more detailed public economic analysis to use in comments and litigation.

how_it_helps.text: The bill changes the Endangered Species Act so that agencies 'shall' — not 'may' — exclude an area from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of inclusion, unless excluding it would cause the species' extinction.

It requires a quantitative and qualitative economic analysis — covering land use, property values, water and power service, employment, and revenues for state and local governments and school districts — to be published for public comment at the same time as any proposed critical habitat designation.

It applies to any habitat designation proposed or finalized on or after October 30, 2013, and requires designations already finalized since that date to be reopened for a new economic analysis within 30 days of enactment.
The economic analysis could not be used to change the underlying decision to list a species as endangered or threatened.

analysis.who_pays: Threatened and endangered species, which would lose protected habitat wherever the economic benefit of excluding land outweighs the conservation benefit; and, indirectly, the public, whose interest in preserving wildlife and the ecosystems that depend on intact habitat would be weakened. Taxpayers would also fund broader economic analyses and the reopening of designations already finalized.

drawbacks.text: Making exclusions mandatory would shrink the habitat protected for endangered and threatened species wherever economic uses of the land are judged more valuable, weakening one of the Act's main recovery tools.
Reopening every habitat designation finalized since October 30, 2013 would create regulatory uncertainty and could unwind protections already in place, at taxpayer expense.

Supporters of current law argue the economic analysis is largely duplicative: agencies already prepare economic analyses of habitat designations and weigh exclusions under existing law, so the bill's practical effect would be to force exclusions rather than improve information.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's transparency element — publishing an economic analysis alongside any proposed habitat rule — is reasonable on its face. But the core change, converting discretionary habitat exclusions into mandatory ones, would shift the Endangered Species Act's balance away from species recovery and toward land development interests, and the retroactive reopening of finalized designations adds uncertainty without adding protection. The costs to conservation fall on the public; the gains are concentrated among landowners and regulated industries.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Mark Pryor of Arkansas introduced the Private Landowner Protection Act of 2014 in the Senate on July 31, 2014, joined by Senator John Boozman, also of Arkansas.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No further action was taken: the committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Threatened and endangered species came out ahead in the narrow sense that habitat designations finalized since October 2013 were not reopened and the mandatory exclusion was never enacted; landowners and regulated industries did not get the relief they sought.

for.name: Sen. Mark Pryor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on July 31, 2014.

for.name: Sen. John Boozman
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after its referral on July 31, 2014, leaving it to die at the end of the 113th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only two sponsors were a Democrat and a Republican, both from Arkansas, so its support was bipartisan but extremely narrow, and no vote ever tested it.

industries.note: Mandatory exclusions would lift critical habitat restrictions on private land wherever the economic benefit of development outweighs the conservation benefit, and the retroactive reopening of finalized designations would give landowners a fresh chance to challenge rules already in place. The gain comes at the cost of weaker habitat protection for endangered species.

The bill requires the economic analysis to cover effects on the provision of power and on federal consultations under section 7 of the Endangered Species Act, and mandatory exclusions could remove habitat barriers to power projects and transmission lines. Reliability for consumers is part of the stated case, but the practical effect is fewer habitat restrictions on utility projects.

The bill requires analysis of habitat designations' effects on water provision and on revenues available to state and local governments and school districts. For water utilities and local governments that face habitat-related limits on water use or infrastructure, more information and possible exclusions could ease costs their ratepayers and residents would otherwise bear.

The bill would shrink protected critical habitat by making exclusions mandatory and would reopen designations already finalized, weakening the Endangered Species Act's main habitat tool on behalf of land use interests.
